parts: Text prepared for publication in "EL Mundo del Perro" magazine, Nº 316, Shih Tzu special issue

The Shih Tzu should be shown at its own natural speed, neither rushed nor pulled upwards by the lead, so that its smooth, flowing, effortless movement can be assessed, with good reach in front and equally strong rear drive, a level, straight back, the head carried naturally high and the tail gracefully curved over the back.
When assessing the Shih Tzu's movement from the front, we should see the front and hind legs moving along the same imaginary line, with no sideways movement of the body.

The forelegs should extend straight from the body, with the front feet turning neither inwards nor outwards, and certainly never crossing; the elbows should remain close to the chest. This action should be smooth and apparently effortless. The dog should move freely and lightly, barely touching the ground.

The head should be held naturally high, not forced upwards by pulling on the lead. This gives the breed its strikingly proud and distinguished bearing, almost arrogant, as though putting on airs of importance.

Viewed from behind, the hind legs should extend powerfully and straight backwards from beneath the body, with the pads of the feet always visible during this extension. There should be perfect vertical alignment between the hips and the pads.

The feet should not fly up into the air; they should remain close to the ground. A hind foot flying up into the air represents wasted effort, as the air provides nothing solid for the dog to push against.

Viewed from the side, movement highlights the balance between the front and rear. We should see a dog whose neck allows proud head carriage, with well-angulated shoulders, a straight back and a tail that curves gently over the back as a result of its set-on. The legs should achieve the greatest possible extension, but without effort.
Taken together, these features give the Shih Tzu graceful movement, as though "floating on a cloud", since the feet spend barely a moment on the ground between each extension and flexion.

Moving faster or slower is not considered a fault. The key is power and balance in movement. Excessive speed in the ring makes it extremely difficult to assess correct movement. If we combine this with excessive pulling on the lead, our Shih will tend to lift its forequarters off the ground.
Our Shih's temperament also influences its movement, as a cheerful dog tends to move better than an apathetic one, carrying its neck higher and showing more animation in the ring.
The abundant coat may make observation difficult or even mislead us, so the dog should be assessed as a whole, with a hands-on examination to complete the assessment.
